description: SMA, polymorph, thermo-chromic, electroluminescent film, QTC and phase-changing materials.
content_html:
What Are Smart Materials?

Smart materials change one of their own properties in response to an environmental stimulus. This response is predictable and usually reversible: remove the stimulus and the material returns to its original state. Smart materials are increasingly used in product design because they can replace complex mechanical components with a simpler, lighter and more responsive material solution.

Shape Memory Alloy (SMA)

Shape memory alloy (SMA) is a metal — typically a nickel–titanium alloy called nitinol — that can be deformed when cool and then returns to its original shape when heated above its transition temperature. This behaviour is useful in medical devices: SMA stents are inserted into blood vessels in a compressed form and then expand to the correct diameter when warmed by body heat, without requiring a mechanical inflation device.

In consumer products, SMA wire is used in eyeglass frames that spring back after being bent, and in thermostatic valves that open automatically when temperature rises. The key examiner point is that SMA is a metal with a recoverable change — not a polymer — and the change requires heat above a specific transition temperature.

Key Fact

Shape memory alloy (SMA) is typically a nickel–titanium alloy (nitinol). It can be deformed when cold and returns to its original shape when heated above its transition temperature. Applications include medical stents, self-straightening eyeglass frames and thermostatic valves.

Polymorph

Polymorph is a thermoplastic material supplied as small white pellets. It becomes soft and mouldable when placed in warm water (approximately 62°C) and can be shaped by hand. When it cools to room temperature it becomes rigid and white. It can be reheated and reshaped repeatedly. Designers use polymorph for rapid prototyping and for creating custom-fit components — for example, custom grips for tools or orthopaedic supports shaped directly to a user’s body.

Thermo-chromic Materials

Thermo-chromic materials change colour when heated or cooled. The colour change is reversible — cool the material down and the original colour returns. They are used in thermometers (the liquid crystal type that changes colour across a temperature range), on baby feeding spoons (indicating when food is too hot), and in novelty mugs and packaging that reveal a graphic when a hot drink is poured in.

Photo-chromic materials change colour in response to light — specifically ultraviolet (UV) radiation. The most familiar application is self-tinting (photochromic) spectacle lenses, which darken outdoors and lighten indoors. Photo-chromic inks are used in security printing and on some packaging to indicate UV exposure.

Key Fact

Thermo-chromic materials respond to temperature; photo-chromic materials respond to light (UV). Both changes are reversible. Common exam error: confusing the stimulus for each type.

Electroluminescent Film

Electroluminescent (EL) film emits light when an electrical current passes through it. The film is thin, flexible and can be produced in large sheets or cut to shape. Applications include: illuminated safety clothing and cycle jackets, backlighting for instrument panels, and low-power decorative lighting in wearable technology. Because it is thin and flexible, EL film can be incorporated into textiles and clothing designs that would not accommodate conventional LED strips.

Quantum Tunnelling Composite (QTC)

Quantum tunnelling composite (QTC) is a flexible, rubber-like material that is normally an electrical insulator. When compressed, conductive metal particles within the material are forced close enough together to allow electrons to ‘tunnel’ through the gaps, making the material conduct electricity. The resistance drops dramatically — and controllably — with pressure. QTC is used in touch-sensitive gloves for touchscreen operation, in pressure sensors for medical devices, and in on/off switches that require no mechanical moving parts.

Modern materials include engineered composites that combine the best properties of two or more constituent materials. Carbon fibre reinforced polymer (CFRP) combines carbon fibre strands (very high stiffness and tensile strength) with a polymer matrix (typically epoxy resin) that binds the fibres and protects them. CFRP is used in aircraft frames, racing car bodies and high-performance bicycle frames because it is stiffer and lighter than steel. Kevlar (para-aramid fibre) is extremely tough and used in body armour, cut-resistant gloves and helmets. Glass-reinforced plastic (GRP) uses glass fibre in a polyester or epoxy resin matrix; it is cheaper than CFRP and used for boat hulls, car body panels and storage tanks. These materials are covered in more depth in the Composites and Technical Textiles lesson.

Phase-Changing Materials

Phase-changing materials (PCMs) absorb large amounts of heat as they melt (change from solid to liquid) and release that heat as they solidify. This behaviour is used in building insulation, packaging for temperature-sensitive pharmaceuticals, and in specialist clothing — where PCM microcapsules embedded in fabric absorb body heat when the wearer is active and release it when the wearer cools down, helping to regulate body temperature.

Nomex and Rhovyl

Nomex is a heat-resistant para-aramid fibre used in protective clothing for firefighters, racing drivers and military personnel. It does not melt or drip when exposed to flame, which prevents the fabric sticking to skin. Rhovyl is a chlorofibre derived from polyvinyl chloride (PVC). It has naturally flame-retardant properties and is used in protective nightwear and bedding, particularly for young children and elderly people. Both are specialist performance fibres rather than general-purpose textiles.

A frequent error is describing thermo-chromic materials as responding to light, or photo-chromic materials as responding to heat. The names contain the clue: ‘thermo’ = heat, ‘photo’ = light. Similarly, students sometimes describe SMA as ‘growing’ or ‘expanding’ when it should be described as ‘returning to its pre-set shape.’ The material does not expand arbitrarily — it returns to one specific memorised geometry. For QTC, the key point is that it is insulating under no pressure but conducts under compression — stating this contrast earns the mark.
exam_tip_html: For smart materials questions, always state the stimulus (what causes the change) and the response (what changes). Thermo-chromic: stimulus = temperature change; response = colour change. Photo-chromic: stimulus = UV light; response = colour change. SMA: stimulus = heat above transition temperature; response = returns to pre-set shape. QTC: stimulus = pressure/compression; response = changes from insulator to conductor. For extended writing on smart materials, include a specific application and explain why that material’s properties make it suitable for that context.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Smart materials respond predictably and reversibly to a stimulus: SMA to heat (returns to pre-set shape), thermo-chromic to temperature (colour change), photo-chromic to UV light (colour change), QTC to pressure (insulator to conductor), EL film to electricity (emits light).
  • Modern materials include composites (CFRP, Kevlar, GRP), phase-changing materials (absorb/release heat on melting/solidifying), and specialist fibres like Nomex (flame-resistant) and Rhovyl (chlorofibre, flame-retardant).
  • In exam answers, always name the stimulus and the response for each smart material — and link the application to why that specific property is useful in that product or context.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes a thermo-chromic material?
A) It returns to a pre-set shape when heated above its transition temperature
B) It changes colour reversibly in response to a change in temperature
C) It becomes electrically conductive when compressed
D) It emits light when an electrical current passes through it
practice_questions.marks: B) It changes colour reversibly in response to a change in temperature [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the stimulus and response for a quantum tunnelling composite (QTC).
practice_questions.marks:
• Stimulus: compression / pressure applied to the material [1 mark]
• Response: changes from an electrical insulator to a conductor [1 mark]
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how shape memory alloy (SMA) behaves when cooled and then heated, and name one application.
practice_questions.marks:
• When cooled (below transition temperature), SMA can be deformed into a new shape (1).
• When heated above its transition temperature, it returns to its pre-set original shape (1).
• Application: medical stent inserted compressed and expands with body heat / self-straightening eyeglass frames / thermostatic valve [any one] (1).
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why polymorph is useful for creating custom-fit product components. Refer to its material properties in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
2 marks per developed point:
• Polymorph becomes mouldable at approximately 62°C (in warm water) (1), allowing a designer or user to shape it by hand to exactly the required form without specialist tools (1).
• When cooled to room temperature it becomes rigid and holds its shape (1), making it suitable for structural components such as grips or supports that need to resist deformation in use (1).
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: A designer is developing a children's spoon that warns parents when food is too hot. Explain, with reference to a smart material, how the spoon could be designed to perform this function without electronic components.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies thermo-chromic material specifically, explains the stimulus (temperature above a set threshold) and the response (colour change), applies this to the spoon context (e.g. handle changes from green to red when food exceeds 40°C), considers safety and reversibility. Appropriate material fully integrated into product function.
Secure: Thermo-chromic correctly identified with stimulus and response explained; spoon context embedded in at least one point.
Developing: Smart material identified but response or stimulus vague; product context limited.
Emerging: General reference to changing colour; no specific material named or mechanism explained.
[6 marks — levels-based]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using shape memory alloy (SMA) in a medical stent compared with a traditional mechanical expanding stent.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced discussion of SMA advantages (no mechanical inflation needed, simpler insertion, responds to body temperature automatically, lightweight, biocompatible nitinol) and disadvantages (precise transition temperature required, cost, potential for incomplete expansion, limited to applications within the temperature range). Traditional stent comparison embedded. Weighted judgement about which is more suitable in which circumstances.
Secure: Two developed advantages and two developed disadvantages; some specific detail (e.g. body temperature, nitinol, biocompatibility); conclusion present.
Developing: Points made but imbalanced or underdeveloped; limited specific material knowledge.
Emerging: Simple list of pros/cons; no medical or material specifics.
[8 marks — levels-based]

knowledge_checks.q: What stimulus causes a shape memory alloy (SMA) to return to its pre-set shape?
Which smart material changes from an electrical insulator to a conductor when compressed?
Photo-chromic materials change colour in response to _____ (UV) radiation, making them suitable for self-tinting spectacle lenses.
Polymorph becomes soft and mouldable at approximately _____ °C when placed in warm water.
Match each smart material to its correct stimulus:
right: Changes colour in response to a temperature change
Emits light when an electrical current passes through it

flashcard_questions.a: A material that responds predictably and reversibly to an environmental stimulus such as heat, light or pressure.

flashcard_questions.q: What alloy is most commonly used as a shape memory alloy (SMA)?
What happens to SMA when heated above its transition temperature?
flashcard_questions.a: It returns to its pre-set original shape.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one medical application of SMA.
flashcard_questions.a: A vascular stent — inserted compressed and expands to the correct diameter using body heat.

flashcard_questions.q: At approximately what temperature does polymorph become mouldable?
What is the stimulus for thermo-chromic materials?
What is the stimulus for photo-chromic materials?
Where are photo-chromic materials most commonly used in everyday products?
flashcard_questions.a: Self-tinting spectacle lenses that darken outdoors and lighten indoors.

flashcard_questions.q: What does electroluminescent (EL) film do when electricity passes through it?
flashcard_questions.a: It emits light — used in illuminated clothing and instrument backlighting.

flashcard_questions.q: What is unusual about QTC's electrical behaviour under compression?
flashcard_questions.a: It changes from an electrical insulator to a conductor as pressure is applied.

flashcard_questions.q: What property makes Nomex suitable for firefighters' protective clothing?
flashcard_questions.a: It does not melt or drip when exposed to flame, preventing fabric sticking to skin.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Rhovyl, and what property makes it useful in protective nightwear?
flashcard_questions.a: Rhovyl is a PVC-derived chlorofibre with natural flame-retardant properties.

flashcard_questions.q: How do phase-changing materials help regulate body temperature in clothing?
flashcard_questions.a: They absorb heat as they melt when the wearer is active, then release it as they solidify when the wearer cools.

glossary_terms.definition: Materials that respond to a change in their environment — such as temperature, light or pressure — by changing one of their own properties in a predictable and reversible way.
A metal alloy that returns to a pre-set shape when heated above its transition temperature, having been deformed at a lower temperature.
A material that changes colour reversibly in response to a change in temperature.
A material that changes colour reversibly when exposed to UV light or a change in light intensity.
A flexible composite material that is an electrical insulator when not compressed but becomes a conductor when squeezed, due to quantum tunnelling of electrons between conductive particles.
